parts.title: Joining a community workshop
parts.instructions: Questions 1–6. Complete the notes. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer. You will hear the recording once. You have 30 seconds to read the questions.
parts.script:
Receptionist: Good morning, Harbour Workshop. How can I help?
Caller: Hello. I saw your poster about the Saturday repair course. Is it mainly for people who already know how to repair bicycles?
Receptionist: No, beginners are welcome. We explain basic maintenance, then you work on your own bike with help from a tutor. We also offer sewing classes, but that is a different course.
Caller: That sounds useful. I thought the repair class was on the fifth of November.
Receptionist: That was our original plan. We have moved it to the twelfth because the tutor is away on the fifth. The nineteenth is a separate gardening session.
Caller: The twelfth, right. What time should I arrive?
Receptionist: The building opens at nine, but the course begins at nine thirty. Please arrive ten minutes before that so we can check your booking. It finishes at twelve.
Caller: And where is the room? My friend said something about a library.
Receptionist: The library is opposite us. We are in the old station building. Use the side entrance beside the cafe, not the main doors. They are closed during renovation.
Caller: Do I need to bring any tools?
Receptionist: We supply tools and gloves. Just bring a notebook so you can record the steps. Wear comfortable clothes, but you do not need any special equipment.
Caller: How much does it cost? I saw eighteen pounds online.
Receptionist: Eighteen is the normal price. Students pay fourteen pounds if they show a student card. Tea is included in both prices.
Caller: I am a student, so fourteen. Can I pay when I arrive?
Receptionist: You can, but you must reserve your place by email. We need the booking no later than Thursday. Please do not wait until Friday: that is when we prepare the materials.
Caller: Thursday, understood. Is there somewhere to leave my bicycle?
Receptionist: Yes, there is secure parking in the courtyard. Bring it into the room after you sign in.
Caller: Great. I will email you today. Thank you.
Receptionist: You are welcome. We look forward to seeing you.

items.prompt: Course date: _____ November
items.evidence: We have moved it to the twelfth
items.rationale: 5 was the cancelled date; 19 refers to gardening. Accept digits or the ordinal, not another date.

items.prompt: Course begins at: _____ (write the time in numbers)
items.evidence: the course begins at nine thirty
items.rationale: 9 is building opening time; 12 is the finishing time. Conventional written time formats are equivalent.

items.prompt: Use the entrance beside the: _____
items.evidence: Use the side entrance beside the cafe
items.rationale: The library is opposite the building, not beside the entrance; the courtyard is parking.

items.prompt: Bring a: _____
items.evidence: Just bring a notebook
items.rationale: Tools and gloves are supplied; the requested item is singular.

items.prompt: Student price: £_____
items.evidence: Students pay fourteen pounds
items.rationale: 18 is the standard price. The pound sign is already printed.

items.prompt: Latest day to email a booking: _____
items.evidence: We need the booking no later than Thursday
items.rationale: Friday is preparation day, not the booking deadline.

parts.title: A student project on shared study rooms
parts.instructions: Questions 7–9: choose ONE answer, A, B or C. Questions 10–12: match each proposed change with its main purpose, A–D. You may use a letter more than once. Read the questions during the opening pause.
parts.script:
Here is a short report on our student project about shared study rooms. We originally wanted to compare examination marks before and after the university opened a new room. That proved impossible: different students used different rooms, and we could not separate the effect of the room from the amount of revision they did. Instead, we investigated which room conditions students associated with being able to concentrate.
We placed a questionnaire online, but most responses came from regular library users. To reach students who rarely entered the library, we also interviewed people in the cafeteria. This did not make our sample fully representative; it simply included some students who were missing from the online responses. We did not offer prizes or ask lecturers to choose participants.
One finding surprised us. Many students described themselves as easily distracted, yet did not choose complete silence as their preferred condition. They wanted a low, steady background sound, such as distant conversation. Sudden noises were the problem. We should be careful, though: a stated preference does not prove that someone learns more effectively in that setting.
The university asked us to suggest three affordable changes. First, coloured signs could mark a quiet zone and a discussion zone. Their purpose is to make expectations clear, not to increase the number of seats. We do not want students to guess whether conversation is acceptable.
Second, we suggested adjustable desk lamps. There is already adequate overhead light, so lamps would let individual users choose the brightness that suits them. Buying more lamps would not reduce interruptions from other students.
Finally, students said that people often returned to a room only to discover that every desk was occupied. A simple occupancy display beside the entrance would help them choose a room before unpacking. It would show the approximate number of free desks, not reserve a particular seat.
We would test these changes for six weeks and repeat the same concentration questions afterwards. We would also record how often each zone was used. We would not claim that a higher satisfaction score was the same as a higher examination result. Our project can guide room design, but it cannot establish that one design causes better academic performance.

items.prompt: What did the project finally investigate?

options.A: Whether a new room improved examination marks
options.C: The number of hours students spent revising

items.evidence: we investigated which room conditions students associated with being able to concentrate
items.rationale: A was abandoned; revision time was a confounding factor, not the revised research question.

items.prompt: Why did the researchers interview students in the cafeteria?

options.A: To include people who rarely used the library
options.C: To let lecturers select a representative sample

items.evidence: To reach students who rarely entered the library, we also interviewed people in the cafeteria
items.rationale: Prizes and lecturer selection are explicitly denied; this did not make the sample fully representative.

items.prompt: What does the speaker caution against assuming?

options.B: Some students prefer steady background sound
options.C: A preferred environment necessarily improves learning

items.evidence: a stated preference does not prove that someone learns more effectively in that setting
items.rationale: A and B are reported findings. Only C is the unsupported inference.

items.prompt: Coloured zone signs — main purpose

options.C: Help users find available space

items.evidence: Their purpose is to make expectations clear
items.rationale: Signs distinguish quiet/discussion behaviour; they do not change lighting or availability.

items.prompt: Adjustable desk lamps — main purpose

options.C: Help users find available space

items.evidence: let individual users choose the brightness that suits them
items.rationale: Only B concerns personal brightness; lamps do not prevent other students interrupting.

items.prompt: Occupancy display — main purpose

options.C: Help users find available space

items.evidence: help them choose a room before unpacking
items.rationale: The display shows free desks. The speaker explicitly says that it does not reserve a seat.

parts.title: When a cooler street is more than a row of trees
parts.instructions: Questions 1–4: TRUE if the statement agrees with the text, FALSE if it contradicts the text, NOT GIVEN if the text does not provide the information. Questions 5–8: choose the paragraph A–E containing the information; a letter may be used more than once. Questions 9–12: complete the notes using NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the text.
parts.text:
A
When a city plans for hotter summers, planting trees may appear to be an obvious solution. A shaded pavement can feel markedly more comfortable than one exposed to direct sunlight. Yet the effect of trees on a street is not determined simply by counting them. Shade changes during the day, depending on the position of the sun and the shape of nearby buildings. A tree that shelters a bus stop at midday may offer little protection to people waiting there late in the afternoon. Planners therefore need to ask where people spend time, not merely where an empty planting space exists.

B
Trees influence their surroundings in two principal ways. Their leaves intercept sunlight, preventing some of it from reaching the surfaces below. They also release water vapour through a process called transpiration. However, the second effect depends on water being available to the roots. During a prolonged dry period, some trees reduce water loss, so their evaporative cooling effect becomes smaller even while their shade remains useful. This does not mean trees cease to provide benefits. It means that a prediction made after rainfall cannot automatically describe conditions at the end of a dry summer.

C
An illustrative street study compared three blocks within the same neighbourhood. One block had mature trees; another had recently planted trees; the third had no trees but included pale paving. Researchers measured air temperature at pedestrian height and used thermal sensors to measure surface temperature. The mature-tree block had much cooler pavement in the afternoon, but its air temperature differed only slightly from that of the other blocks. The pale paving reflected more sunlight and also had a relatively cool surface. Some pedestrians nevertheless reported discomfort because reflected light reached them directly. A surface that is cooler to the touch is not necessarily a more comfortable place to stand.

D
The study also exposed a problem with simple comparisons. The tree-lined block contained lower buildings and received more wind than the other two. Its residents had agreed to reduce car parking, leaving more soil uncovered. Any difference between the blocks could therefore reflect several changes acting together. Rather than attributing every result to trees alone, the researchers proposed measuring the same sites before and after specific changes. They also suggested comparing several similar streets. Such work would take longer, but it would distinguish an attractive explanation from a well-supported one.

E
Practical decisions require more than temperature measurements. In one planning exercise, residents marked the routes they regularly used to shops, clinics and bus stops. The busiest routes were not always those with the highest recorded temperatures. People caring for children or carrying shopping valued uninterrupted shade along a route more than a small, very cool area that required a detour. The planners consequently prioritised continuity of shade. They also checked that new planting would not obstruct wheelchair access or conceal road crossings. Cooling was one aim among several: a comfortable route still had to be usable and safe. The lesson was not that measurement was unhelpful, but that numbers needed to be interpreted alongside everyday activity.

items.prompt: Counting trees alone is enough to predict a street's cooling benefit.
items.evidence: not determined simply by counting them
items.rationale: A explicitly contradicts sufficiency of tree count; this is not missing information.

items.prompt: A shortage of water can reduce trees' evaporative cooling.
items.evidence: their evaporative cooling effect becomes smaller
items.rationale: B explicitly links this reduction to a prolonged dry period.

items.prompt: The mature-tree block had a substantially lower afternoon air temperature than the other blocks.
items.evidence: its air temperature differed only slightly
items.rationale: The large change concerns pavement, not air; substantially lower air temperature contradicts C.

items.prompt: Most residents in the planning exercise travelled to work by bus.
items.evidence: routes they regularly used to shops, clinics and bus stops
items.rationale: E gives destinations but no majority, commuting purpose or travel mode.

items.prompt: Which paragraph explains why a cool surface may still cause pedestrian discomfort?

options.C: C

items.evidence: reflected light reached them directly
items.rationale: Only C distinguishes reflected radiation and surface temperature.

items.prompt: Which paragraph identifies several differences that complicate a comparison?

options.C: C

items.evidence: lower buildings and received more wind
items.rationale: D also names uncovered soil and parking; C describes measurements, not the confounders.

items.prompt: Which paragraph describes a shade benefit changing with the time of day?

options.C: C

items.evidence: little protection to people waiting there late in the afternoon
items.rationale: A specifically contrasts midday and later shade at a bus stop.

items.prompt: Which paragraph incorporates users' journeys into planning?

options.C: C

items.evidence: residents marked the routes they regularly used
items.rationale: A asks where people spend time, but only E actually maps their journeys.

items.prompt: Trees release water vapour through _____.
items.evidence: a process called transpiration
items.rationale: The process is explicitly named in B; evaporation is not the term supplied in the text.

items.prompt: Researchers measured the pavement using _____.
items.evidence: used thermal sensors to measure surface temperature
items.rationale: Air temperature was measured separately; the plural two-word instrument is required.

items.prompt: Residents valued continuous shade rather than a cool space requiring a _____.
items.evidence: required a detour
items.rationale: The completion asks for the diversion, not another route destination.

items.prompt: New planting had to preserve _____ access.
items.evidence: would not obstruct wheelchair access
items.rationale: Only wheelchair qualifies access in the text; road crossings are a separate safety check.

parts.title: Riverside Community Centre: visitors and volunteers
parts.instructions: Questions 1–4: choose ONE answer, A, B or C. Questions 5–8: TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN, using only the text. Questions 9–12: complete each answer using NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the text.
parts.text:
VISITING RIVERSIDE
The Riverside Community Centre opens from 8.30 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays. On Saturdays it opens at 10 a.m. and closes at 4 p.m.; it is closed on Sundays. Reception closes thirty minutes before the building, so arrive earlier if you need help registering for a course. People attending an evening class may still enter after reception closes if they already have a booking confirmation.

The downstairs reading room is free to use. It is reserved for quiet individual work from opening time until 2 p.m. After 2 p.m., small groups may use the tables for discussion. Please use headphones for audio at all times. Food is not allowed, but drinks in sealed containers are permitted. The upstairs meeting room is available for private hire. Booking that room does not give a group exclusive use of the downstairs reading room.

There is a small car park behind the centre. Its four spaces are reserved for drivers displaying a valid disability parking permit. Other visitors should use the public car park beside the market, a five-minute walk away. Bicycles may be locked to the racks near the main entrance. Please do not leave them in the corridor, even for a short visit.

Visitors can cancel a paid course booking up to seven days before the first session and receive a full refund. Later cancellations receive a credit for another course, except when the centre itself cancels: in that case the original payment is refunded. If you miss a session after the course has begun, no refund or credit is available for that session.

VOLUNTEERING AT RIVERSIDE
We need volunteers for our Saturday repair mornings. No repair experience is necessary for reception duties. Volunteers who want to assist with electrical repairs must first complete our safety training. Do not assume that previous work experience replaces this requirement. Volunteers are not permitted to test electrical equipment on their own.

New volunteers attend an induction on the first Wednesday of the month, from 6 p.m. to 7 p.m. If you cannot attend, email the volunteer coordinator to arrange the next available induction; do not arrive for a Saturday shift before completing one. Bring photo identification to the induction. There is no charge for attending.

At each shift, sign the attendance sheet at reception before putting on your name badge. If you notice damaged tools, stop using them, label them clearly and tell the session supervisor. Place them in the locked cupboard only when the supervisor tells you to. Never leave damaged tools with working tools.

Shift requests are submitted through the volunteer portal by Monday evening. The coordinator publishes the confirmed rota on Thursday. A request is not a confirmed shift. If you need to withdraw after the rota is published, contact the coordinator directly so a replacement can be found; changing your portal request alone is not enough. Travel expenses can be claimed monthly using the centre's expense form. Include receipts for public transport. The centre does not reimburse meals bought during a shift.

items.prompt: When does reception close on Saturday?
items.evidence: Reception closes thirty minutes before the building
items.rationale: Saturday building closure is 4 p.m.; subtract 30 minutes. C applies on weekdays.

items.prompt: What may visitors do in the reading room before 2 p.m.?

options.C: Eat while attending a private meeting

items.evidence: reserved for quiet individual work
items.rationale: Discussion is only after 2 p.m.; food is prohibited and private hire concerns upstairs.

items.prompt: Where should a driver without a disability permit park?

options.B: At the public car park beside the market
options.C: Near the bicycle racks

items.evidence: Other visitors should use the public car park beside the market
items.rationale: The rear spaces require a permit; the racks are for bicycles.

items.prompt: A visitor cancels three days before a course begins. What is offered?

options.B: A credit for a different course
options.C: Nothing under any circumstances

items.evidence: Later cancellations receive a credit for another course
items.rationale: Three days is inside the seven-day window; centre cancellation, not visitor cancellation, gives a late refund.

items.prompt: Reception volunteers must already know how to repair equipment.
items.evidence: No repair experience is necessary for reception duties
items.rationale: Explicit contradiction; electrical assistance has different requirements.

items.prompt: Experienced electrical repair workers may skip the centre's safety training.
items.evidence: Do not assume that previous work experience replaces this requirement
items.rationale: Training applies regardless of previous experience.

items.prompt: The induction is free.
items.evidence: There is no charge for attending
items.rationale: The statement directly follows induction instructions.

items.prompt: Most volunteers travel to Riverside by public transport.
items.evidence: Include receipts for public transport
items.rationale: The expense rule says nothing about how many volunteers use that transport.

items.prompt: What document must volunteers sign before wearing their badge?
items.evidence: sign the attendance sheet
items.rationale: The expense form and rota are different documents with different purposes.

items.prompt: Who must be told about damaged tools?
items.evidence: tell the session supervisor
items.rationale: The coordinator organises shifts, not tool safety; the shortened role remains unambiguous.

items.prompt: On which day is the confirmed rota published?
items.evidence: publishes the confirmed rota on Thursday
items.rationale: Monday is the request deadline; Wednesday is induction.

items.prompt: What proof must accompany a public transport expense claim?
items.evidence: Include receipts for public transport
items.rationale: The plural proof is explicitly requested; the form is the claim document, not supporting proof.

parts.title: Preparing a short exhibition
parts.instructions: Questions 13–15: complete the notes using ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER. Questions 16–18: choose ONE answer, A, B or C. This is additional screening evidence, not a second full test.
parts.script:
We have made a few changes to the exhibition plan. Please take notes so we all use the same information. The exhibition will open on the eighteenth of March, not the fifteenth as our first poster said. The fifteenth is now the day we install the displays. It will be held in the gallery, because the main hall is needed for another event.
We were going to charge four pounds at the door. The community fund has now covered the room hire, so admission will be free. Donations are welcome, but visitors are not required to make one.
Our main problem last year was not the number of visitors. Plenty of people came, but many left without understanding how the objects had been selected. This year, each display needs a short explanation of the connection between its objects. Do not simply add a longer list of dates. We want visitors to understand the idea behind the selection.
Please keep labels brief. Use one everyday example to explain an unfamiliar term rather than removing every technical word. Specialists may recognise the original term, while other visitors can use the example. The aim is to make the display accessible without making it inaccurate.
Before printing all the labels, we will ask a small group of visitors to read a draft and explain the message in their own words. If they misunderstand the main idea, we will revise it. We are not testing whether they can remember the exact wording. We are checking that our explanation communicates what we intended.
Bring your draft labels to the meeting on Tuesday. We will agree on the final layout then. Thank you.

items.prompt: Opening date: _____ March
items.evidence: open on the eighteenth of March
items.rationale: 15 is installation, not opening.

items.prompt: Venue: the _____
items.evidence: held in the gallery
items.rationale: The main hall is unavailable.

items.prompt: Admission will be _____.
items.evidence: admission will be free
items.rationale: Four pounds is the superseded proposal; donations are optional.

items.prompt: What was the main problem with last year's exhibition?

options.B: Visitors did not understand the selection of objects
options.C: There were not enough historical dates on labels

items.evidence: many left without understanding how the objects had been selected
items.rationale: A is denied; adding dates is specifically not the solution.

items.prompt: How should labels handle unfamiliar technical terms?

options.C: Explain them through an everyday example

items.evidence: Use one everyday example to explain an unfamiliar term
items.rationale: Neither banning terminology nor leaving it unexplained meets the stated aim.

items.prompt: Why will visitors read draft labels?

options.A: To check whether the intended message is understood
options.B: To test memory of the precise wording
options.C: To decide how much admission should cost

items.evidence: checking that our explanation communicates what we intended
items.rationale: Exact recall is explicitly excluded; admission has already been settled.

parts.title: Measuring repair rather than replacement
parts.instructions: Questions 13–15: TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN. Questions 16–18: choose ONE answer, A, B or C.
parts.text:
A survey of household appliances asked owners what they had done when a device stopped working. In the first questionnaire, respondents could choose only 'repaired' or 'replaced'. Interviews later showed that several households had done neither: they had put the broken device in a cupboard and postponed the decision. Excluding this group exaggerated the proportion of immediate replacements. The researchers therefore added 'stored without a decision' to the next questionnaire.

Cost was frequently mentioned, but it was not the only obstacle to repair. Some owners could not discover whether spare parts were available. Others were unsure whom to trust with a repair. A lower price would not necessarily resolve either difficulty. The researchers suggested that clear information about parts and reliable repair services might be as important as a subsidy.

One retailer offered a repair voucher with each new purchase. More voucher holders booked a repair than customers without one. However, voucher holders had bought a different range of products, and some had chosen the retailer because they already valued repair. The comparison could not establish that the voucher itself changed behaviour. A fairer trial would offer the same voucher to a randomly selected group of otherwise similar customers.

The researchers also warned against measuring success only by the number of repairs. A repair that fails after a week differs from one that extends a product's life for several years. They proposed recording how long repaired products continued to be used. This would not answer every environmental question, but it would offer a more useful measure than simply counting completed workshop jobs.

items.prompt: The first questionnaire included all the actions households had taken.
items.evidence: several households had done neither
items.rationale: Storage/postponement was omitted from the first binary question.

items.prompt: Reducing repair prices alone might not remove every obstacle.
items.evidence: A lower price would not necessarily resolve either difficulty
items.rationale: Parts information and trust are separate obstacles.

items.prompt: The retailer's voucher was worth more than the average repair cost.
items.evidence: offered a repair voucher with each new purchase
items.rationale: Neither voucher value nor average repair cost is given.

items.prompt: Why did the first survey overestimate immediate replacement?

options.B: It left out owners who postponed a decision
options.C: It interviewed only repair businesses

items.evidence: Excluding this group exaggerated the proportion of immediate replacements
items.rationale: The omitted group stored broken devices; double counting and business-only sampling are not described.

items.prompt: What limits the conclusion about the voucher?

options.A: The two customer groups differed in other ways
options.B: None of the vouchers were used
options.C: The retailer refused to supply spare parts

items.evidence: had bought a different range of products
items.rationale: Prior motivation also differed. B contradicts increased bookings; C is not stated.

items.prompt: Which measure of repair success do the researchers prefer?

options.A: The number of workshops in each town
options.C: The length of continued product use

items.evidence: recording how long repaired products continued to be used
items.rationale: The proposed outcome is durability of use, not counts of businesses or incentives.

parts.title: A workplace equipment trial
parts.instructions: Questions 13–15: TRUE, FALSE or NOT GIVEN. Questions 16–18: choose ONE answer, A, B or C.
parts.text:
STAFF NOTICE: ADJUSTABLE DESKS
From 3 November, the customer support team will trial six adjustable desks for four weeks. This is a trial, not a permanent allocation. Staff may volunteer by emailing the office manager before 28 October. If there are more than six volunteers, names will be selected at random; length of service will not affect selection.

Each selected volunteer must attend a twenty-minute demonstration before using a desk. Even if you have used a similar desk elsewhere, this demonstration is required because the controls may differ. The facilities team will record the desk's height settings and check the cables. Do not move a desk yourself or place heavy boxes underneath it.

Participants should alternate between sitting and standing when comfortable. There is no requirement to stand all day. If discomfort develops, return to sitting and inform the office manager. If a control fails, unplug the desk and report the fault to facilities; do not attempt a repair.

At the end of the trial, participants will complete a short questionnaire about comfort and ease of use. They will not be assessed on the number of calls they handled. The company will decide whether to buy more desks only after reviewing the feedback and maintenance costs. Participation does not guarantee that a volunteer will keep their trial desk. Staff who are not selected can request a separate review of their current seating at any time.

items.prompt: Employees with longer service have priority if too many people volunteer.
items.evidence: length of service will not affect selection
items.rationale: Random selection explicitly excludes seniority preference.

items.prompt: Everyone selected must attend the demonstration, including experienced desk users.
items.evidence: Even if you have used a similar desk elsewhere, this demonstration is required
items.rationale: There is no experience exemption.

items.prompt: The new desks cost less than the company's current desks.
items.evidence: reviewing the feedback and maintenance costs
items.rationale: The notice mentions costs but gives no price comparison.

items.prompt: What should a participant do if standing becomes uncomfortable?

options.A: Continue standing until the shift ends
options.B: Sit down and notify the office manager
options.C: Adjust the desk cables without help

items.evidence: return to sitting and inform the office manager
items.rationale: Standing all day is not required; cables are checked by facilities.

items.prompt: What should happen if a desk control stops working?

options.B: It should remain plugged in for the trial
options.C: The desk should be unplugged and the fault reported

items.evidence: unplug the desk and report the fault to facilities
items.rationale: Self-repair is explicitly prohibited; continuing powered use is not advised.

items.prompt: What determines whether more desks are purchased?

options.B: The number of calls made by volunteers
options.C: A promise already made to every volunteer

items.evidence: only after reviewing the feedback and maintenance costs
items.rationale: Call counts are excluded; no retention or purchase guarantee is given.

writing.prompt: Some people believe that learning a practical skill is more effective in a small face-to-face group. Others prefer learning independently through online resources. Which approach do you think is more effective, and why? Explain your view and consider one benefit of the other approach. Use reasons and an example from your experience or observation.
writing.instructions: Write about 160–200 words in 16 minutes. This is a short readiness sample, not a full official IELTS essay. Answer both parts, organise your ideas and leave time to check your writing. Your teacher will review the response; there is no automatic IELTS band.

rubric.label: Task response
rubric.foundation: The position is unclear, a required part is missing, or ideas remain disconnected assertions.
rubric.conditional: A relevant view and the alternative benefit are present, but explanation or examples are thin.
rubric.ready: A clear view addresses both parts, with relevant reasoning and a developed example.

rubric.label: Organisation and connection
rubric.foundation: The reader struggles to follow the sequence; sentence links frequently obscure meaning.
rubric.conditional: The main sequence is understandable; paragraphing or links sometimes feel mechanical or unclear.
rubric.ready: Ideas progress logically through focused paragraphs and clear links, without excessive signposting.

rubric.label: Vocabulary
rubric.foundation: A narrow range or frequent word-choice errors repeatedly limits the message.
rubric.conditional: Everyday vocabulary communicates the main ideas, with repetition or occasional imprecision.
rubric.ready: A sufficient range conveys distinctions and examples accurately; occasional slips do not obscure meaning.

rubric.label: Sentence control
rubric.foundation: Frequent basic errors or fragments make several sentences difficult to understand.
rubric.conditional: Simple sentences are generally clear; attempts at more complex structures are uneven.
rubric.ready: Simple and more complex sentences are controlled well enough to express reasoning clearly.

speaking.examinerInstructions: Conduct this check in person. Confirm identity and explain that this is internal readiness screening, not an official IELTS band assessment. Do not teach, correct language, suggest vocabulary or score from accent alone. Allow a brief repeat of a question without simplifying it. Keep the fixed timings. Record specific observed strengths and difficulties. If access needs, illness, noise or interruption limit the evidence, mark insufficient evidence and arrange another check rather than assigning a low language rating.
familiarQuestions: Do you currently work, study, or do something else? What does a typical day involve?
What is one skill you would like to learn? Why?
When you learn something new, do you prefer working with other people or on your own?
Tell me about a place where you can concentrate well.

longTurn.prompt: Describe a time when you learnt something useful outside a formal class.
bullets: how and where you learnt it
and explain why learning it was useful to you.
longTurn.instruction: Give the candidate the cue card, paper and a pencil. Allow one minute for notes, then say: Please begin. I will stop you after about a minute and a half. Do not interrupt except at the time limit.

followUp: Why do some people find it difficult to keep learning after leaving school?
How can workplaces help employees learn without disrupting their work?
Can online resources replace a skilled teacher? Why or why not?
Is making mistakes an important part of learning? When might mistakes be less acceptable?

rubric.label: Fluency and coherence
rubric.foundation: Long breakdowns prevent sustained answers or a connected account.
rubric.conditional: The candidate develops short answers but needs noticeable planning pauses or loses the thread.
rubric.ready: The candidate sustains a connected account and explains views despite some natural hesitation.

rubric.label: Vocabulary
rubric.foundation: Limited words or failed paraphrases repeatedly prevent communication.
rubric.conditional: Familiar topics are communicated adequately; abstract discussion exposes repetition or gaps.
rubric.ready: The candidate explains and paraphrases sufficiently across familiar and more general questions.

rubric.label: Sentence control
rubric.foundation: Frequent basic errors repeatedly make intended relationships unclear.
rubric.conditional: Simple structures communicate meaning; more complex attempts are inconsistent.
rubric.ready: A usable mix of structures expresses relationships clearly; errors seldom disrupt understanding.

rubric.label: Intelligibility
rubric.foundation: The listener repeatedly cannot recover words or phrases without substantial effort.
rubric.conditional: Most speech is understandable, but individual sounds, stress or phrasing sometimes require effort.
rubric.ready: Speech is consistently intelligible with helpful phrasing; a regional accent is not a weakness by itself.

scoringNotes: Each objective item earns one mark. Completion spelling must match an explicitly accepted alternative after case/whitespace normalisation; no fuzzy matching. Missing or wrong answers earn zero. Meaningful singular/plural distinctions remain unless an alternative is listed. Use the private per-item rationales for marking disputes. This original short screen is not psychometrically validated and has no official IELTS-band conversion. Teacher Writing and Speaking review determines final placement.
